channel.title: PsyDigest — psychiatry literature digest
channel.description: Summaries of new psychiatric research and guidelines

item.title: [25] Antipsychotic Co-Initiation Versus Monotherapy Initiation for People with Acute/Exacerbated Schizophrenia Spectrum Disorders: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The clinical question is whether adding a second antipsychotic at the start of treatment (co-initiation) speeds recovery in acute schizophrenia compared with starting one drug (monotherapy). The study is a systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in adults with acute/exacerbated schizophrenia-spectrum disorders.
FINDINGS: Across 15 RCTs (n=1 937, mean age 32 y, 61 % male, mean follow-up 10 weeks), co-initiation increased the chance of treatment response (RR 1.28, 95 % CI 1.11–1.48; moderate certainty). Total symptom reduction favoured co-initiation (SMD –0.35, 95 % CI –0.71 to 0.00; low certainty) and negative symptoms improved (SMD –0.55, 95 % CI –1.08 to –0.02; low certainty). No clear benefits were seen for positive symptoms, depression, quality of life or global severity. Adverse effects and discontinuation rates were similar between groups.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests a modest short-term advantage of co-initiation for overall response and negative symptoms, but the effect sizes are small and certainty is low for most outcomes. The trials were at moderate risk of bias (missing data) and often underpowered; 28 % dropped out. Therefore, the clinical gain is uncertain and may not outweigh the risks of polypharmacy.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not justify routine co-initiation; if tried, it should be time-limited, monitored closely for side-effects, and re-evaluated within 1–2 weeks.

item.title: [15] Generative AI Chatbot Responses to Suicide and Self-Harm: Systematic Review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review (PRISMA-guided, registered protocol) examined how generative AI chatbots respond to user disclosures of suicide or self-harm, a clinically important question as chatbots are increasingly used for mental health support. It synthesized 29 empirical studies (2020–2025) across audit, development, and adversarial designs, focusing on safety and quality of responses.
FINDINGS: Of 1,042 records, 29 studies were included (16 published, 13 preprints). Most evaluated proprietary models (23/29), often using synthetic single-turn prompts (23/29) and auditing suicidal content only (21/29). Proprietary models (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude) generally provided higher-quality responses than open-weight or companion models, but this advantage weakened in sensitivity analyses. Chatbots frequently offered emotional support but often gave generic, context-lacking replies, rarely assessed risk, and performed poorly with ambiguous or moderate disclosures. Responses were inconsistent, often requiring multiple turns to recommend crisis resources or human support. Under adversarial "jailbreaking," harmful responses were common.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is preliminary and heterogeneous, with many preprints, small samples, and synthetic prompts limiting generalisability. Methodological quality varied, and rapid model iteration complicates reproducibility. While proprietary models may outperform others in some domains, the clinical impact remains uncertain due to lack of real-world, multiturn, or stakeholder-informed studies. The risk of harmful outputs under adversarial conditions is a notable safety concern.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current chatbots may offer emotional validation but are unreliable for risk assessment, escalation, or consistent crisis referral. Clinicians should caution patients about using chatbots for suicidal ideation, especially under adversarial conditions, and prioritise evidence-based care pathways. More real-world research is urgently needed before integrating chatbots into suicide prevention strategies.

item.title: [14] Association between remitted major depressive disorder and subsequent risk of cognitive deficit and neurocognitive disorders - A systematic review and meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study addresses whether a history of remitted major depressive disorder (rMDD) in older adults is associated with cognitive deficits or later diagnoses of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) or dementia. It is a systematic review and meta-analysis of 28 non-overlapping studies (6,512 rMDD; 60,493 healthy controls).
FINDINGS: Among 24 studies assessing cognitive performance, 79% (19/24) found worse performance in rMDD versus controls across seven domains. Six studies reporting diagnostic outcomes showed mixed results (3/6 supporting higher MCI/dementia risk). Meta-analysis of 24 studies showed significantly poorer global cognition in rMDD (effect sizes not reported in abstract). Heterogeneity was high.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests an association between rMDD and late-life cognitive deficits, but diagnostic risk findings are inconsistent. High heterogeneity and lack of effect sizes in the abstract limit precision. Funding sources and study quality are not mentioned, so confidence should be moderate. Further high-quality longitudinal studies are needed to determine causality and clinical significance.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings support individualized cognitive risk assessment in older adults with a history of rMDD, but do not yet justify routine screening or preventive interventions based solely on depression history.

item.title: [14] Patients', family members' and healthcare professionals' attitudes towards medical assistance in dying on psychiatric grounds: systematic review of qualitative literature.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Medical assistance in dying on psychiatric grounds (MAiD-PS) raises complex ethical and clinical questions. This preregistered systematic review and metasynthesis of qualitative studies synthesised attitudes of patients, family members, and healthcare professionals across countries, aiming to identify convergences and divergences in perspectives.
FINDINGS: Twelve qualitative studies (2018–2024) were included. The metasynthesis identified 15 themes. Patients and family members emphasized individual self-determination and dignity, while healthcare professionals highlighted relational autonomy and the clinical difficulty of assessing irremediability. Despite thematic overlap, conceptual differences were evident in how each group framed MAiD-PS.
INTERPRETATION: The review is based on a transparent, preregistered search and synthesis using established qualitative methods. However, the included studies are heterogeneous in setting and sample, and the review does not quantify attitudes or assess risk of bias beyond methodological quality screening. The findings are preliminary and exploratory, reflecting attitudes in specific contexts rather than generalizable prevalence. The contrast in perspectives underscores the need for inclusive dialogue in guideline development.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This review highlights the importance of incorporating diverse stakeholder voices into policy discussions on MAiD-PS. Clinicians should be aware of differing priorities across groups when discussing MAiD-PS with patients and families, but should not assume uniformity within groups.

item.title: [12] Cardiovascular Risk Associated With Psychostimulant Therapy in Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder: A Systematic Review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review (registered in PROSPERO) assessed cardiovascular safety of psychostimulants for ADHD by synthesising 52 studies and six guidelines, aiming to inform prescribing clinicians and cardiologists about screening and risk stratification.
FINDINGS: Psychostimulants caused small increases in heart rate and systolic blood pressure but showed no significant increase in myocardial infarction, stroke, or sudden cardiac death in healthy populations. Evidence in older adults and those with cardiovascular comorbidities was limited and suggested potential risk. Current guidelines advise baseline history and examination without routine ECG or cardiology referral unless red flags are present, but these guidelines are outdated and mainly paediatric-focused.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is moderate in size but largely observational, limiting causal inference. Strengths include comprehensive literature search and guideline review; limitations include heterogeneity of studies and lack of robust data in older or comorbid patients. The proposed age- and risk-stratified framework addresses gaps in current guidance but remains to be validated prospectively.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: For young, healthy patients, routine ECG screening is not supported; focus on history and examination. For patients over 50–65 or with cardiovascular comorbidities, individualised risk assessment and possible ECG/ cardiology referral should be considered.

item.title: [11] Modulating cognitive reappraisal and hedonic capacity to alleviate depressive symptoms: A randomized controlled fNIRS-based neurofeedback intervention study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This randomized controlled trial (RCT) examined whether functional near-infrared spectroscopy neurofeedback training (fNIRS-NFT) targeting right lateral prefrontal cortex (LPFC) activity could alleviate depressive symptoms in adults with depression, and whether changes in cognitive reappraisal and hedonic capacity mediated these effects. The study included 88 participants, with 59 receiving the intervention and 29 as no-intervention controls, and followed outcomes for three months.
FINDINGS: Among those completing fNIRS-NFT (n=59), only the high-improvement (HI) subgroup (n=37) showed significant reductions in depressive symptoms (BDI scores) compared to controls, with effects sustained at three-month follow-up. Mediation analyses indicated that fNIRS-NFT enhanced cognitive reappraisal, which increased hedonic capacity, sequentially reducing depressive symptoms. Changes in LPFC activity correlated with improvements in hedonic capacity and cognitive reappraisal (CSCA and RSA analyses).
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests potential efficacy of fNIRS-NFT in a subgroup of patients, but the lack of randomization to HI/LI stratification and the absence of blinding introduce risk of bias. The small sample size and reliance on self-report measures (BDI) limit generalizability. While the mechanistic pathway is plausible, confirmatory trials with active controls and larger samples are needed to validate clinical utility.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings do not justify routine use of fNIRS-NFT for depression outside research settings. Clinicians should await larger, well-controlled trials before considering this intervention, while noting that mechanisms involving cognitive reappraisal and hedonic capacity may inform future therapeutic targets.

item.title: [11] A Structured Exercise Intervention for Individuals With Psychotic Disorders Treated With Long-Acting Injectable Antipsychotics: Protocol for a Nonrandomized Controlled Study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study protocol outlines a prospective, controlled, longitudinal trial to evaluate whether a 24-week supervised multimodal exercise program can improve psychotic symptomatology and metabolic outcomes in 151 adults (mean age 46.4 years) with psychotic disorders receiving long-acting injectable (LAI) antipsychotics. The design is nonrandomized, allocating participants to exercise versus treatment-as-usual.
FINDINGS: The trial is ongoing; as of May 2026, 25 of 151 participants had been enrolled. Outcomes will be assessed at baseline, 12 weeks, 24 weeks, and 8-week follow-up. Primary outcomes include psychotic symptoms and metabolic measures (body composition, cardiometabolic risk). Exploratory biomarker analyses (BDNF, dopamine, serotonin) and antipsychotic treatment patterns will also be examined. Funding was secured in January 2026; data analysis is planned for December 2026.
INTERPRETATION: This is a protocol with no results yet, so internal validity cannot be judged. The nonrandomized design risks selection bias and confounding. External validity may be limited by the single-center setting and inclusion of stable outpatients on LAIs. If positive, the effect size on psychotic symptoms and metabolic outcomes remains unknown. Biomarker analyses are exploratory and should be interpreted cautiously.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: No clinical implications can be drawn until efficacy data are available. Clinicians should await peer-reviewed results before considering integrating supervised multimodal exercise into routine care for this population.

item.title: [10] Engaging Communities in FASD Research: A Systematic Review of Community Engaged Research Through the Lens of Empowerment Theory and REACH Tool.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review examined how community engaged research (CEnR) has been implemented in prenatal alcohol exposure (PAE) and fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) studies, using Empowerment Theory and the REACH Tool to assess engagement levels and phases. The review aimed to characterize methods, benefits, barriers, and facilitators of CEnR in this field.
FINDINGS: Fifty-one studies were included. Most engaged communities during data collection at the consult level, where input was gathered but final decisions remained with researchers. Reported barriers included structural, logistical, relational, ethical, and methodological challenges. Facilitators included trust building, flexibility, community ownership, and ethical practices. Perceived benefits were cultural relevance, increased trust, improved recruitment/retention, and relevance of findings. Empowerment was applied both as a process and an outcome.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is descriptive and based on qualitative synthesis of heterogeneous studies, limiting causal inference. Strengths include a comprehensive search and use of structured tools (REACH, Empowerment Theory). However, reliance on author-reported benefits and lack of standardized engagement metrics reduce internal validity. External validity is constrained by the specific PAE/FASD context, though findings may generalize to other stigmatized neurodevelopmental conditions. The clinical significance remains uncertain as no quantitative effect sizes or direct patient outcomes were reported.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This review highlights CEnR as a potentially valuable approach for improving research relevance and trust in PAE/FASD, but it does not provide direct evidence for changing clinical practice. Clinicians should be aware of CEnR as an ethical and methodological framework, but should await more rigorous studies linking CEnR to improved patient outcomes before adopting it as a standard practice.

item.title: [9] Examining mindfulness-based exercises, relaxation practices and Strategies for Safety and Well-being in English primary and secondary schools (INSPIRE): multi-school, cluster-randomised controlled trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The INSPIRE trial was a cluster-randomised controlled trial (cRCT) in UK primary and secondary schools evaluating three school-based mental health interventions—mindfulness-based intervention (MBI), relaxation-based practice intervention (RBPI), and Strategies for Safety and Well-being (SSW)—against usual practice. The study aimed to assess whether these interventions improved emotional difficulties (MBI, RBPI) or intended help-seeking (SSW) in pupils aged 8–13 years over 3–6 months.
FINDINGS: A total of 213 schools (20,489 pupils) were randomised. In primary schools, MBI (n=3732) showed no effect on emotional difficulties (SMD 0.002, 95% CI -0.08 to 0.08), and RBPI (n=3731) also showed no effect (SMD -0.01, 95% CI -0.10 to 0.07). SSW (n=3453) improved intended help-seeking (SMD 0.09, 95% CI 0.01–0.18). In secondary schools, neither MBI (n=3791, SMD -0.07, 95% CI -0.18 to 0.05) nor RBPI (n=3531, SMD -0.10, 95% CI -0.24 to 0.02) improved emotional difficulties, and SSW (n=3762) showed no effect on help-seeking (SMD 0.07, 95% CI -0.03 to 0.18).
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests that MBI and RBPI do not reduce emotional difficulties in either primary or secondary school pupils, and SSW shows no benefit in secondary schools. The small but statistically significant improvement in help-seeking with SSW in primary schools (SMD 0.09) is of uncertain clinical significance. The study’s large sample size and cluster-randomised design strengthen internal validity, but the short follow-up and reliance on self-reported outcomes limit conclusions about long-term impact. No major adverse effects were reported, but potential biases in school-level randomisation and variability in intervention delivery across schools are concerns.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support implementing MBI or RBPI in schools to reduce emotional difficulties in this age group. SSW may modestly improve help-seeking intentions in primary school children, but the effect is small and requires replication. Clinicians should remain cautious about recommending these interventions based solely on this trial’s findings.

item.title: [9] Mind over metabolism: a systematic review of GLP-1 receptor agonists in the treatment of stress-related disorders.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review examined whether glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) agonists, already licensed for type 2 diabetes, could be repurposed for stress-related psychiatric disorders (depression and PTSD). The review synthesised preclinical rodent studies and early-phase human “experimental medicine” trials to assess translational rationale.
FINDINGS: Forty-three studies (28 rodent, 15 human) were included. Across agents, results were heterogeneous; some small human studies showed modest improvements in depressive or anxiety symptoms, while others showed no benefit. Exenatide findings were especially inconsistent and appeared to depend on neurobiological context and concomitant medications. No trials specifically tested GLP-1R agonists for PTSD; data were limited to anxiety- or stress-related outcomes.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is preliminary and inconsistent. Study designs are heterogeneous, sample sizes are small, and no high-quality randomised controlled trials in clearly defined psychiatric populations exist. Therefore, confidence in any therapeutic effect is low. Any potential benefit may be confined to patients with comorbid metabolic dysfunction, but this remains unproven.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: At present, GLP-1R agonists cannot be recommended for routine treatment of depression or PTSD outside of clinical trials. Clinicians should remain alert to emerging trial data but should not change practice based on current evidence.

item.title: [9] Vibrotactile stimulation selectively enhances motor memory consolidation in adults with ADHD: A diagnosis-specific effect.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Can a non-pharmacological vibrotactile stimulation (VtSt) during motor learning improve overnight consolidation in adults with ADHD? This randomized study tested VtSt added to motor sequence training in 97 young adults (65 ADHD, 32 controls) across acquisition, 24-hour consolidation, and 1-week retention phases.
FINDINGS: Acquisition was unaffected by VtSt. A significant Diagnosis × Condition × Timepoint interaction (p = 0.006) showed that in ADHD, VtSt improved overnight consolidation (p = 0.025, Cohen’s d = 0.40) with a trend to 1-week retention (p = 0.060). Re-presenting VtSt at 1 week acutely boosted performance (p = 0.020). In ADHD, chronotype (β = 0.289, p = 0.024) and VtSt condition (β = 0.334, p = 0.010) predicted consolidation gains; controls showed no VtSt benefit.
INTERPRETATION: This is an adequately powered RCT with clear diagnosis-specific effects and modest effect sizes (d ≈ 0.40). Strengths include the longitudinal design and prespecified predictors; limitations include unmedicated ADHD sample, short follow-up, and lack of actigraphy-based sleep measures predicting gains. The clinical significance of a 0.4 SD improvement is uncertain until replicated in real-world settings and clinically meaningful outcomes.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: VtSt may offer a low-risk adjunct to motor learning in adults with ADHD, especially for those with evening chronotype, but evidence is preliminary; routine adoption awaits larger, longer trials measuring functional outcomes.

item.title: [9] Ketamine to treat depression and the wish to hasten death in advanced cancer patients: The KODIAC pilot study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT (KODIAC pilot) tested intravenous ketamine as an adjunct to standard antidepressants in 19 inpatients with advanced cancer, major depressive disorder (MDD) and a wish to hasten death (WTHD). The study asked whether two ketamine infusions would reduce depressive symptoms and WTHD more than placebo.
FINDINGS: In the intention-to-treat sample (n=19), ketamine reduced the BEDS-Mx score from 13.6 to 4.6 versus 13.3 to 11.7 with placebo (p=0.0018) and the SAHD-Mx score from 4.0 to 0.5 versus 3.7 to 3.6 (p=0.0093) across visits 1–4. Per-protocol results were similar (n=12; BEDS-Mx p=0.0001; SAHD-Mx p=0.00001). No serious adverse events were reported.
INTERPRETATION: The trial is small (n≈20) and terminated early, so estimates are imprecise and at high risk of random error. The double-blind design and use of validated scales strengthen internal validity, but the absence of an active comparator and short follow-up (four visits) limit conclusions on durability and generalisability. The reported p-values are statistically significant, yet the clinical magnitude—especially for WTHD—remains uncertain given the tiny sample and lack of effect-size reporting.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These preliminary data suggest ketamine may rapidly reduce depressive symptoms and WTHD in this highly selected group, but the evidence is insufficient to change routine practice; larger, longer trials with active comparators and robust safety monitoring are needed before any bedside change.

item.title: [8] Worry as a mechanism of change in internet-delivered cognitive-behavioral therapy for generalized anxiety disorder.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examined whether worry acts as a mechanism of change in therapist-guided internet-delivered cognitive-behavioral therapy (iCBT) for generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) using a large routine-care sample (n=8,870; 78.2% women). It applied dynamic modeling to test directional relationships between worry, anxiety-related impairment, and somatic GAD symptoms during a 12-session iCBT program.
FINDINGS: Non-Gaussian direction-of-dependence analysis showed worry predicted later anxiety-related impairment across sessions. Continuous-time structural equation modeling (CT-SEM) revealed bidirectional feedback between worry and somatic symptoms, with somatic symptoms also reducing subsequent worry. CT-SEM further suggested unobserved common causes may explain part of the worry–somatic symptom link.
INTERPRETATION: The large, real-world sample and sophisticated dynamic modeling strengthen causal inference relative to small RCTs. However, observational within-treatment data cannot prove causation; unmeasured confounders and feedback loops complicate interpretation. The modest effect sizes and absence of a comparator arm limit clinical inference. Findings align with the contrast-avoidance model but remain preliminary until replicated in controlled trials.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence supports monitoring worry as a potential treatment target in iCBT for GAD, but does not yet justify changing standard protocols. Clinicians should watch for reciprocal somatic–worry cycles during therapy and consider tailoring techniques accordingly.

item.title: [8] From shared genetic liability to druggable biology in suicide risk.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This integrative genomics study asks whether shared genetic liability across suicide-related phenotypes can be resolved into biologically coherent dimensions and whether druggable targets can be nominated for suicide prevention. The work combines structural equation modeling, transcriptome-wide association, and AI-driven virtual ligand screening in a multi-step translational pipeline.
FINDINGS: Genomic SEM supported a single latent genetic liability linking suicide-related traits with psychiatric, environmental, socioeconomic, and pain phenotypes. This liability split into two interpretable dimensions—endogenous affective risk and exogenous stress. Six core risk genes (TM9SF4, SUSD3, PTPDC1, VPS33B, XRCC3, LSM10) were prioritized by convergent TWAS and fine-mapping. Five candidate ligands targeting TM9SF4 showed stable binding in molecular dynamics simulations and favorable binding free-energy scores; seven additional gene–tissue links were identified via pQTL/eQTL colocalization.
INTERPRETATION: The study is hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory. Strengths include the multi-modal integration of large-scale genomic and transcriptomic data and the use of structural biology tools to shortlist ligands. However, the findings are entirely computational and pre-clinical; no experimental validation in human tissue, animal models, or clinical samples is reported. Effect sizes and statistical thresholds for gene prioritization are not provided in the abstract, so the magnitude and robustness of the associations remain uncertain. External validity is unclear because the genomic dimensions were derived from GWAS of predominantly European-ancestry cohorts and may not generalize to other populations.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: At present, this work does not change bedside practice. It suggests TM9SF4 and related pathways as potential research targets, but clinical utility awaits functional validation, safety profiling, and trials before any treatment implications can be considered.

item.title: [7] Effects of Online and Offline Psychotherapies on Anxio-Depressive Symptom Severity in Depression and Anxiety Disorders: A Follow-Up Research in Hungary.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study compared the effectiveness of online versus in-person psychotherapy for reducing anxio-depressive symptoms in adults with depression or anxiety disorders during the COVID-19 pandemic, using a quasi-experimental design with non-randomized group allocation based on patient preference. The clinical question is whether online synchronous psychotherapy is comparable to traditional in-person care in routine settings.
FINDINGS: Fifty-six participants were assessed at baseline, mid-treatment (6th session), and post-treatment. Both groups showed significant reductions in depressive symptoms (BDI), anxiety (STAI), health anxiety (SHAI), and general psychological symptoms (SCL-90-R). No statistically significant differences were found between online and offline modalities in symptom reduction. Baseline differences were limited to higher life event scores in the offline group (p=0.042). Effect sizes were not reported.
INTERPRETATION: The study has moderate internal validity due to its quasi-experimental design, lack of randomization, and potential selection bias (patients chose modality based on preference). The absence of blinding and reliance on self-report measures further limit validity. External validity is constrained by a small, non-representative sample and high attrition, particularly in the online group. While both modalities showed symptom improvement, the lack of equivalence testing and high dropout preclude firm conclusions about noninferiority. The findings suggest potential effectiveness of online therapy but should be interpreted cautiously.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Online psychotherapy may be a viable option for motivated patients with mild-to-moderate depression or anxiety who prefer remote care, but current evidence does not support equivalence to in-person therapy. Clinicians should monitor engagement and consider patient preferences when selecting treatment modality. Further high-quality RCTs are needed before changing practice.

item.title: [7] Violet Light-Induced Changes in Voice Vitality Indices and Their Associations With Sleep Improvement in Patients With Depression.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This exploratory sub-analysis of a sham-controlled, double-blind randomized crossover trial examined whether violet light (VL) irradiation alters voice vitality indices and whether these changes relate to sleep improvement in adults with mild major depressive disorder (MDD). The study tested whether voice-derived vitality indices could serve as non-invasive biomarkers of treatment response.
FINDINGS: In 38 adults with mild MDD, active VL significantly improved the depression-specific vitality index (vitality-depression) versus sham (significant time-by-intervention interaction), while the overall vitality index (vitality-all) showed no significant interaction. Higher baseline vitality-all correlated with greater sleep improvement (PSQI reduction) under active VL, but the difference from sham was not statistically significant. In a multiple regression model controlling for covariates, higher baseline vitality-all predicted greater sleep improvement (β = −0.41, p = 0.04), whereas higher baseline vitality-depression predicted less sleep improvement or worsening (β = 0.38, p = 0.03).
INTERPRETATION: The findings suggest VL may modulate vocal biomarkers linked to mood and sleep, but the evidence is preliminary. The crossover design and double-blinding strengthen internal validity, though the small sample (n=38) and exploratory nature limit generalizability. The observed associations between vitality indices and sleep improvement are statistically significant but of uncertain clinical magnitude, and replication in larger, more diverse samples is needed before considering voice biomarkers for routine use.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support changing practice based on voice vitality indices. Clinicians should await larger validation studies before considering these measures for monitoring depression or sleep outcomes in routine care.

item.title: [7] War-related post-traumatic stress disorder among conflict-affected civilians: an umbrella review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This umbrella review synthesised systematic reviews and meta-analyses to estimate the prevalence of war-related PTSD among conflict-affected civilians (refugees, internally displaced persons, non-displaced residents) and appraised the methodological quality of the evidence. The clinical question is how common PTSD is in these populations and how reliable the estimates are.
FINDINGS: Eighteen reviews (12 meta-analyses) covering five world regions reported PTSD prevalence ranging from 11.6% (Lebanon) to 61.9% (Iraqi IDPs). Re-analysis of six reviews gave a pooled prevalence of 28.0% (95% CI 22.0–34.9%; I² = 87.8%), with displaced/refugee populations at 43.7% (95% CI 24.6–65.0%) versus 23.4% (95% CI 20.3–26.7%) in general samples. No review was rated high quality; three were moderate, six low, and nine critically low.
INTERPRETATION: Confidence in the pooled prevalence is low because AMSTAR 2 ratings were predominantly “critically low,” and heterogeneity (I² = 87.8%) was extreme. The wide CIs and methodological flaws (e.g., variable diagnostic thresholds, selection bias) limit comparability across conflicts and populations. The markedly higher burden in displaced groups is consistent with prior literature but remains imprecisely estimated.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The findings support routine screening and provision of trauma-focused care in humanitarian settings, especially for displaced populations, while highlighting the urgent need for standardized diagnostic methods and higher-quality research to guide policy and practice.

item.title: [6] Perinatal suicide risk factors: A network analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This cross-sectional registry study (N=20,217) used U.S. National Violent Death Reporting System data to map how life circumstances cluster around perinatal suicide decedents versus non-perinatal decedents, applying network analysis to 18 binary indicators across relationships, health, socioeconomic status, and suicide risk factors.
FINDINGS: The analytic sample comprised 1,297 perinatal and 18,920 non-perinatal decedents. In the overall network, perinatal status connected mainly to intimate partner problems; in the perinatal-only network, postpartum status linked to depressed mood and mental health diagnoses. Depressed mood showed the highest bridge betweenness in both networks, and physical health and socioeconomic domains were consistently connected.
INTERPRETATION: The study’s cross-sectional design and reliance on proxy indicators limit causal inference. Network stability was modest in the perinatal subgroup, so bridge centrality estimates should be interpreted cautiously. The findings highlight correlates rather than causal pathways, suggesting that suicide prevention in childbearing-aged women may need to address broader life domains beyond pregnancy itself.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should screen perinatal women not only for mood symptoms but also for intimate partner problems, physical health issues, and socioeconomic stressors; however, these associations do not yet justify specific preventive interventions without further prospective validation.

item.title: [24] Effectiveness of Psychosocial Interventions to Promote Mental Health and Psychological Well-Being Among Older Persons With Depression and Anxiety: Systematic Review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review examined the effectiveness of psychosocial interventions for promoting mental health and psychological well-being among older adults (≥65 years) with depression and/or anxiety. The review included RCTs published between 2015 and December 2025, addressing a gap in synthesizing diverse psychosocial treatments in this population.
FINDINGS: From 2,830 screened records, 27 RCTs were included, covering 11 distinct psychosocial interventions (e.g., CBT, behavioural activation, reminiscence therapy). All interventions reduced depressive symptoms, while 6 reduced anxiety symptoms, and 5 improved psychosocial well-being/quality of life. Effect sizes varied widely by intervention type and setting, with CBT, behavioural activation, and reminiscence therapy most frequently studied and effective. No meta-analysis was performed due to heterogeneity in outcomes and insufficient numerical data.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is moderate in size but highly heterogeneous, limiting firm conclusions about comparative effectiveness. The lack of meta-analysis and reliance on narrative synthesis reduce precision in estimating effect sizes. While results suggest psychosocial interventions are beneficial, the variability in outcomes and settings underscores the need for tailored, context-specific approaches. Funding sources were not reported, and study quality appraisal (MMAT-18) suggests potential risk of bias in some included trials.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Psychosocial interventions (particularly CBT, behavioural activation, and reminiscence therapy) may be considered for older adults with depression/anxiety, but treatment selection should be individualized based on patient preferences, cultural context, and local resources. Further high-quality RCTs with standardized outcomes are needed to clarify optimal interventions and effect sizes.

item.title: [20] A Perspective on Adjunctive/Combination Therapy in Major Depressive Disorder: What Have We Learned from Studies of Atypical Antipsychotics?
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines adjunctive/combination therapy with atypical antipsychotics in major depressive disorder (MDD), focusing on study designs, outcomes, and reporting inconsistencies across trials. It synthesizes pivotal trials and systematic reviews to highlight unmet needs and propose future directions.
FINDINGS: Eight atypical antipsychotics were studied as adjuncts or in combination with antidepressants; six had industry sponsorship and regulatory approvals (OFC for TRD; aripiprazole, brexpiprazole, cariprazine, lumateperone, quetiapine-XR for inadequate response). Study designs varied widely in inclusion/exclusion criteria and response assessment, and publications showed inconsistent reporting. Systematic reviews/meta-analyses often pooled heterogeneous studies, limiting comparability.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is methodologically fragmented, with design heterogeneity and inconsistent reporting undermining synthesis. While several agents show efficacy in narrowly defined populations, the lack of standardized methodologies and transparent reporting reduces confidence in indirect comparisons and network meta-analyses. The review underscores the need for collaborative, standardized trial frameworks to improve validity and generalizability.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current practice relies on heterogeneous, often industry-sponsored trials; clinicians should interpret adjunctive antipsychotic use in MDD cautiously, considering patient-specific factors and the limited generalizability of existing evidence. Standardized future trials are needed before firm practice changes can be recommended.

item.title: [19] Synaptic Vesicle Glycoprotein 2A and Excitatory-Inhibitory Balance in Psychiatric Disorders: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined how synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A (SV2A) expression and modulation influence kindling development in animal models, aiming to clarify SV2A’s role in excitatory-inhibitory balance relevant to psychiatric disorders. Thirty experimental animal studies were synthesized.
FINDINGS: Kindling increased hippocampal SV2A expression, particularly in GABAergic neurons. Genetic reduction of SV2A function increased susceptibility to kindling. Pharmacological or genetic interventions targeting SV2A significantly reduced seizure severity (Hedge g = -2.16; 95% CI, -2.95 to -1.37; P < .001; I2 = 82.3%) and lowered odds of reaching kindling criteria (odds ratio, 0.04; 95% CI, 0.02 to 0.08; P < .001; I2 = 0.4%).
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests SV2A is dynamically regulated by neuronal activity and may act as a compensatory mechanism to restore synaptic homeostasis after repeated excitation. However, high heterogeneity in seizure severity outcomes (I2 = 82.3%) and reliance on animal models limit direct translation to human psychiatric conditions. The clinical significance of these findings remains uncertain until replicated in human studies.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings do not yet justify changes in clinical practice but highlight SV2A as a potential biomarker for circuit resilience in disorders with excitatory-inhibitory dysregulation. Further research in humans is needed to determine whether SV2A PET could guide treatment strategies.

item.title: [18] Cost-utility study of cognitive-behavioural management of auditory hallucinations in schizophrenia: a study protocol.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study is a randomized controlled trial (RCT) protocol evaluating whether a structured cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT) program for auditory verbal hallucinations (AVHs) in patients with schizophrenia spectrum disorders improves clinical outcomes and is cost-effective compared to treatment as usual (TAU). The trial will recruit 240 outpatients aged 15–60 years with distressing AVHs for at least three months.
FINDINGS: The primary outcome is the incremental cost-utility ratio at 12 months, measured as cost per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) using the EQ-5D-5L. Secondary outcomes include changes in AVH severity, depressive symptoms, suicidal ideation, quality of life, functioning, sleep quality, substance use, psychiatric comorbidity, medication exposure, and adherence at 4, 8, and 12 months. Independent evaluators blinded to treatment allocation will conduct assessments.
INTERPRETATION: This is a well-designed RCT with strengths including randomization, stratification by illness severity, and blinded outcome assessment. However, as this is a protocol, no results are available yet. The study’s external validity will depend on recruitment from routine outpatient services and the generalizability of the CBT program’s structure. The clinical significance of the findings will hinge on whether the observed effects are both statistically significant and clinically meaningful, particularly in reducing AVH-related distress and improving quality of life.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: If the CBT program demonstrates cost-effectiveness and clinical benefit, it could support broader implementation of CBT for AVHs in routine psychiatric care, potentially reducing reliance on antipsychotics alone. Clinicians should await the trial results before considering changes to practice.

item.title: [15] Younger Among Peers, Higher at Risk? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Relative Age Effect on ADHD Diagnosis and Treatment.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis investigated whether children who are relatively younger within their school cohort (relative age effect) are more likely to receive an ADHD diagnosis or treatment. The study synthesised data from multiple observational studies to quantify this association.
FINDINGS: The meta-analysis included 28 studies (31 reports) with a total of 4,404 records screened. Children with a younger relative age had a significantly higher odds of ADHD diagnosis (OR = 1.209, 95% CI: 1.044–1.400, p = 0.011) and ADHD treatment (OR = 1.133, 95% CI: 1.031–1.245, p = 0.01).
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests a modest but statistically significant association between relative age and ADHD diagnosis/treatment, with ORs just above 1.0. The included studies are observational, raising concerns about unmeasured confounding (e.g., teacher expectations, parental concerns, or regional diagnostic practices). The effect sizes are small and may not reflect clinical significance. Heterogeneity across studies and potential publication bias were not assessed in the abstract, limiting certainty. The findings highlight a potential systemic bias in ADHD diagnosis rather than a true increase in ADHD prevalence.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should be aware that younger relative age within a school cohort may influence ADHD diagnostic and treatment decisions. However, the small effect size suggests this should not alter clinical practice alone; rather, it underscores the need for careful, age-adjusted evaluation of ADHD symptoms. Further research is needed to determine whether this bias leads to overdiagnosis or inappropriate treatment.

item.title: [14] Clozapine beyond schizophrenia: an umbrella systematic review of the off-label uses of clozapine in managing psychiatric, neurological, and behavioural conditions.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This umbrella systematic review appraised 20 published systematic reviews on off-label uses of clozapine for psychiatric, neurological, and behavioural conditions other than schizophrenia. The review aimed to assess the breadth and quality of evidence supporting these uses.
FINDINGS: Six meta-analyses showed large effect sizes for clozapine in Parkinson’s psychosis (SMD = –4.23; 95% CI –6.53 to –1.93), tardive dyskinesia (SMD = –2.56, p = 0.02), insomnia (OR = 0.45, p < 0.01), substance use disorder (OR = 0.10, p < 0.00001), suicidality (OR = 0.229, p < 0.0001), and mortality (RR = 0.43, 95% CI 0.34–0.55). Additional systematic reviews reported benefits in treatment-resistant bipolar disorder, borderline personality disorder, catatonia, BPSD, and aggression. Confidence ratings were high in 7 reviews, moderate in 3, low in 3, and critically low in 7.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is heterogeneous and of variable quality, with several reviews rated as low or critically low confidence. The strongest signals (Parkinson’s psychosis, suicidality, mortality) come from small meta-analyses with wide confidence intervals, suggesting fragility. Many indications rely on narrative systematic reviews without meta-analysis, limiting quantitative certainty. Funding sources are not reported, which may introduce bias.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clozapine may be considered for Parkinson’s psychosis and severe, treatment-refractory aggression or suicidality when standard care fails, but only after careful risk–benefit discussion and monitoring for adverse effects. Current guidelines should be cautiously updated to reflect these findings, prioritising high-risk, treatment-resistant cases.

item.title: [13] Perioperative neurocognitive disorders in elderly orthopedic surgery: from mechanistic insights to risk prediction and multimodal integrated care.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review addresses perioperative neurocognitive disorders (PND) in elderly orthopedic surgery patients, including delirium and cognitive decline, by synthesizing epidemiological, mechanistic, predictive, and interventional evidence. It distinguishes formal diagnoses from screening-score changes and evaluates orthopedic-specific versus transferable perioperative studies.
FINDINGS: Multicomponent delirium prevention and coordinated perioperative assessment show the strongest clinical support. Large trials such as REGAIN, ENGAGES, and ketamine and minocycline trials reported neutral outcomes for delirium or cognitive prevention. Smaller studies on dexmedetomidine, PENG block, intranasal insulin, TEAS, rTMS, and probiotics show signals that require replication and safety evaluation. Observational hemodynamic and biomarker findings do not establish preventive efficacy.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is limited by the narrative review design, lack of quantitative synthesis, and reliance on heterogeneous, often small or observational studies. High-quality randomized trials with standardized neurocognitive outcomes are needed. Current recommendations rest on multicomponent delirium prevention frameworks rather than definitive orthopedic-specific cognitive protection. The clinical significance of signals from smaller studies remains uncertain.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current practice should prioritize guideline-recommended multicomponent delirium prevention in elderly orthopedic patients. Novel interventions (e.g., dexmedetomidine, PENG block, rTMS) are not yet supported for routine use; further trials are required before adoption. Focus on individualized supportive care and standardized cognitive assessment remains key.

item.title: [13] Psychedelics and Psychedelic-Inspired Compounds for Substance Use Disorders: Are We Treating the Disease or Opening a Learning Window?
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines whether psychedelics (e.g., psilocybin, ketamine, ibogaine) treat substance use disorders (SUDs) directly or transiently enhance learning and treatment engagement. It synthesizes preclinical and clinical evidence across SUDs, focusing on relapse prevention mechanisms and compound-specific risks.
FINDINGS: The review highlights that relapse prevention involves multiple processes (e.g., extinction learning, clinical abstinence), and translational concordance varies by compound and indication. The strongest human evidence supports psilocybin for tobacco and alcohol use disorders, but this rests on two small randomized trials with conflicting results. Ibogaine’s cardiotoxicity and ketamine’s reinforcing properties limit their clinical utility.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is preliminary and heterogeneous, with no clear class effect of psychedelics for SUDs. The review’s narrative approach lacks systematic rigor, and the small, discordant trials for alcohol and tobacco use disorders weaken conclusions. Compound-specific risks (e.g., cardiotoxicity) further constrain applicability. More robust, larger RCTs with standardized outcomes are needed to determine efficacy and safety.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not justify routine use of psychedelics for SUDs outside research settings. Clinicians should remain cautious about off-label use due to unresolved safety concerns and limited efficacy data.

item.title: [12] Bipolar Disorder Literacy: Protocol for a Scoping Review of Assessment Tools and Reported Literacy Levels.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This scoping review protocol aims to map instruments used to assess bipolar disorder (BD) literacy across populations and synthesize reported literacy levels, addressing a gap in understanding how awareness and misconceptions about BD influence early recognition and help-seeking. The study follows PRISMA-ScR guidelines and will include 111 peer-reviewed primary studies identified through searches in MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, and CINAHL.
FINDINGS: The review registered on OSF (DOI: 10.17605/OSF.IO/9E3MF) completed literature search and study selection in July 2026, with data charting and synthesis finalized by September 2026. The manuscript is expected by December 2026. No results are presented in this protocol; findings will be organized by population group and instrument type.
INTERPRETATION: As a scoping review protocol, this study outlines a rigorous methodology to identify and synthesize BD literacy assessment tools and reported levels. The strength lies in its comprehensive search strategy and adherence to PRISMA-ScR guidelines. However, since no results are provided, the clinical implications remain speculative. The review will highlight gaps in measurement and knowledge, but its utility depends on the quality and heterogeneity of included studies and the robustness of the synthesis.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This review could inform the selection of BD literacy assessment tools and guide educational interventions for patients, caregivers, and healthcare professionals, potentially improving early recognition and reducing diagnostic delays. However, until the results are published, its direct impact on clinical practice is uncertain.

item.title: [12] Acceptance and Commitment Therapy for Pregnant Women: A Scoping Review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Pregnancy is a period of increased vulnerability to psychological distress, and Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) has been proposed as a third-wave CBT approach to improve well-being. This scoping review maps the scope and characteristics of ACT-based interventions for pregnant women, summarizing 14 studies involving 862 participants.
FINDINGS: Fourteen studies (2015–2025) with 862 participants (mean age 29.7 years; mean gestational age 28.8 weeks) were included: 8 quasi-experimental, 4 RCTs, and 2 mixed-methods. Outcomes were heterogeneous (24 outcomes, 37 measures), with ACT showing potential benefits for psychological flexibility and symptom reduction, but with substantial variability in intervention delivery and assessment.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is preliminary and heterogeneous, with no consistent standardized protocols or robust long-term follow-up. The lack of detailed reporting on intervention development and fidelity limits reproducibility. While ACT appears promising, the current evidence does not yet support definitive clinical recommendations.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: ACT may be considered as an adjunctive option for pregnant women with psychological distress, but clinicians should be cautious due to limited high-quality evidence and variability in intervention delivery. Further well-designed RCTs with standardized outcomes and longer follow-up are needed before ACT can be routinely recommended.

item.title: [11] Association of Low-Dose Ketamine and Ketamine-Midazolam Administration with Postpartum Depressive Symptoms, Postoperative Pain, and Adverse Events in Cesarean Deliveries Under Spinal Anesthesia.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This prospective, nonrandomized, controlled observational cohort study in 300 women undergoing cesarean delivery under spinal anesthesia examined whether low-dose ketamine (0.5 mg/kg) alone or combined with midazolam (0.01 mg/kg) after umbilical cord clamping was associated with lower postpartum depressive symptoms (EPDS), reduced postoperative pain (VAS), and adverse events.
FINDINGS: At postpartum week 4, median EPDS scores were lower in both ketamine (p = 0.032) and ketamine–midazolam groups versus controls; positive EPDS screening (≥11) occurred in 15%, 17%, and 30%, respectively (p = 0.017). Both treatment groups had lower VAS pain scores at 2 and 4 h and longer time to first rescue analgesia (all p < 0.001). Hallucinations were more frequent with ketamine alone (32%) than ketamine–midazolam (18%) or control (2%) (p < 0.001).
INTERPRETATION: The study suggests potential benefits of low-dose ketamine (with or without midazolam) on short-term postpartum mood and early postoperative pain, but the nonrandomized design, symptom-based group assignment, and lack of blinding introduce confounding by indication and selection bias. Effect sizes are modest and adverse events (notably hallucinations) are common, especially with ketamine alone. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require confirmation in randomized trials with adequate power and safety monitoring.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence is insufficient to change routine practice; any off-label use should be cautious, with informed consent regarding hallucination risk and close monitoring for mood changes.

item.title: [11] [Guidelines in Practice: Delirium in Older Adults - Implications for Anesthesiologists].
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This is a guideline summary (S3 level) from Germany on delirium in older adults, focusing on perioperative and ICU relevance for anesthesiologists. It addresses prevention, diagnosis, and treatment across the care pathway in multimorbid, frail hospitalized patients.
FINDINGS: The guideline recommends structured risk screening (including preoperative assessment) and regular screening (e.g., Nu-DESC) in at-risk patients. Prevention involves multicomponent programs; routine pharmacological prophylaxis is not advised, and benzodiazepines should be avoided. Treatment prioritizes addressing underlying causes, with antipsychotics reserved for distressing symptoms.
INTERPRETATION: As a guideline, the strength lies in its comprehensive, evidence-based recommendations, but its applicability depends on local implementation feasibility (e.g., staffing, documentation burden). The lack of pharmacological prophylaxis recommendation aligns with prior evidence, emphasizing non-pharmacological strategies. However, the abstract does not provide effect sizes or comparative data, limiting assessment of clinical impact.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Anesthesiologists may adjust practice by avoiding benzodiazepine premedication, reviewing anticholinergics, and using EEG monitoring for anesthetic titration. Non-pharmacological measures in the PACU are emphasized, but resource constraints may hinder full implementation.

item.title: [9] Examining the impact of genome-wide findings for tobacco use through GWAS-impact analysis: a systematic review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review examines how genome-wide association study (GWAS) findings on tobacco use (Liu et al., 2019, identifying 406 loci) have been used in subsequent research, assessing translational impact and methodological uptake across phenotypes. It includes 345 studies citing the original GWAS up to June 2023, focusing on analytical approaches and clinical applications.
FINDINGS: Of 345 included studies, 72% used Mendelian randomization, 124 focused on whole-body interventions (e.g., BMI), and 100 on mental/neurodevelopmental disorders. Only 3 studies explored clinical applications. Methodological reporting was inconsistent: 38.8% did not specify which GWAS summary statistic version was used, and only 6.4% used the version excluding UK Biobank participants.
INTERPRETATION: The review highlights substantial research activity leveraging tobacco GWAS data, particularly for causal inference via Mendelian randomization, but reveals a striking translational gap with minimal clinical application. Limitations include inconsistent methodological reporting and reliance on summary statistics without clear version control, which may affect reproducibility. The lack of standardized phenotyping and few clinical evaluations limits assessment of real-world utility.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current GWAS-derived tobacco genetics has not yet demonstrated clear clinical value beyond existing risk assessment tools. Clinicians should be cautious about overinterpreting genetic findings for tobacco use in practice until validated clinical applications emerge and reporting standards improve.

item.title: [9] Evidence for anterior cingulate cortex glutathione levels as a biomarker of oxidative stress and antioxidant response in people with bipolar disorder.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examined whether glutathione (GSH) levels in the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) could serve as a biomarker of oxidative stress in bipolar disorder (BD) and whether N-acetylcysteine (NAC) increases ACC GSH levels. It included a cross-sectional comparison of BD patients (n=29) versus healthy controls (HC, n=26) and a pilot randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind crossover trial (n=12) testing 3 g/day NAC vs. placebo.
FINDINGS: BD patients had significantly higher dorsal ACC (dACC) GSH levels than HC (Cohen’s d = 0.56, p = 0.046), and higher dACC GSH correlated with more past-year depressive episodes (r = 0.39, p = 0.041). In the crossover trial, NAC increased dACC GSH versus placebo (Cohen’s d = 0.45, p = 0.040), but did not change glutamate levels (p = 0.325).
INTERPRETATION: These findings are preliminary due to small sample sizes and should be interpreted cautiously. The cross-sectional association and modest effect sizes in the NAC trial suggest a potential oxidative stress signal in BD, but replication in larger, adequately powered studies is needed. The lack of effect on glutamate argues against a broad neurometabolite change, focusing interest on GSH-specific pathways.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence is insufficient to change practice; dACC GSH may be a future mechanistic biomarker or treatment target, but confirmatory trials with clinical endpoints are required before any bedside application.

item.title: [9] Substantial Treatment-Seeking Interest, Narrow Eligibility: Diagnostic Heterogeneity and External Validity in the PRIDE Psilocybin Trial-Relevance to Precision Psychiatry.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examines the gap between treatment-seeking individuals interested in psychedelic-assisted psychotherapy and the narrow eligibility criteria of clinical trials, using aggregate screening data from the PRIDE trial (a phase II RCT of psilocybin vs. personalized neuromodulation for treatment-resistant depression, TRD) in Italy. The clinical question is whether trial recruitment reflects real-world patient heterogeneity, which matters for the external validity of psychedelic research.
FINDINGS: Among 67 telephone-screened candidates (Nov 2025–Jun 2026), 80.6% (54/67) were excluded, 11.9% (8/67) enrolled and treated, and 7.5% (5/67) were preliminarily eligible. The leading exclusion reason was lack of protocol-defined TRD or another psychiatric diagnosis (50.0%, 27/54), followed by age outside range (18.5%), current suicidal ideation (13.0%), and substance use disorder (9.3%).
INTERPRETATION: This cross-sectional descriptive analysis highlights a substantial mismatch between treatment-seeking interest and trial eligibility, with only ~12% of screened individuals enrolling. The study’s strength is its real-world screening context, but it provides no data on treatment outcomes or individualized selection. Limitations include small sample size, single-site data, and lack of long-term follow-up. The findings underscore concerns about external validity in psychedelic trials, suggesting that results may not generalize to broader clinical populations.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should recognize that current psychedelic trials for TRD enroll a highly selected minority of interested patients, and trial results may not apply to patients with diagnostic heterogeneity or active suicidality. These findings support cautious interpretation of emerging psychedelic evidence until broader, more inclusive trials are conducted.

item.title: [8] Predicting Treatment Resistance in First-Episode Psychosis Using Routinely Collected Clinical Data.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study asks whether routinely collected clinical data at first-episode psychosis (FEP) can predict later treatment resistance (TR), defined by clozapine initiation within 8 years. A prognostic model was developed and validated using electronic health records (EHRs) from 10 NHS trusts in the UK, including 25 665 patients diagnosed between 1998 and 2014.
FINDINGS: The model achieved a mean leave-one-trust-out C statistic of 0.71 (95% CI 0.68–0.75) for predicting clozapine initiation, with a positive predictive value (PPV) of 0.15 (95% CI 0.12–0.17) and a negative predictive value (NPV) of 0.96 (95% CI 0.95–0.97). When using a broader TR definition (clozapine or ≥3 antipsychotics), discrimination dropped to a C statistic of 0.68 (95% CI 0.64–0.72), with PPV 0.27 (95% CI 0.24–0.31) and NPV 0.89 (95% CI 0.88–0.91).
INTERPRETATION: The model shows acceptable discrimination for predicting clozapine initiation, particularly in ruling out future TR (high NPV), but modest PPV suggests many predicted cases may not develop TR. Strengths include large, real-world EHR data and external validation across multiple trusts. Limitations include reliance on clozapine initiation as a proxy for TR, potential unmeasured confounding, and lack of clinical outcome validation beyond medication exposure. The effect size is statistically meaningful but not large enough to guide individual treatment decisions without further refinement.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This model could support early identification of patients at higher risk of TR, potentially enabling earlier clozapine initiation. However, current performance metrics suggest it should be used as an adjunct to clinical judgment rather than a standalone decision tool. Further validation in prospective settings and evaluation of clinical impact are needed.

item.title: [7] Adaptation and Pilot Testing of a Mindfulness-Based Insomnia and Symptom Management Intervention for Women with Breast Cancer in Rural Areas.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This study adapted and pilot-tested a mindfulness-based insomnia and symptom management intervention (Nite2Day) originally designed for hematologic cancer patients, targeting women with breast cancer in rural areas where symptom burden (insomnia, fatigue, distress, pain) is disproportionately high. The pilot used a single-arm design (N=15) to assess feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary changes in patient-reported outcomes.
FINDINGS: The accrual target was met within 6 months, with no attrition (15/15 completed intervention and post-treatment assessments). Acceptability was high (mean score 30.53/32). Pre-post changes in insomnia symptoms, fatigue, distress, pain, pre-sleep arousal, mindfulness, and symptom management self-efficacy all trended in the expected direction (e.g., reduced insomnia severity, improved mindfulness). Qualitative feedback led to protocol refinements (e.g., clearer mindfulness definitions, adjusted session timing).
INTERPRETATION: The study demonstrates feasibility and acceptability of Nite2Day in this population, with no major methodological flaws in this small pilot. However, the single-arm design precludes causal inference, and the lack of a control group means observed improvements could reflect placebo, natural recovery, or regression to the mean. The sample size (N=15) is too small to assess clinical significance or durability of effects. Funding sources and blinding status are not reported, and generalizability is limited by the rural, breast cancer-specific context.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These preliminary results suggest Nite2Day may be a feasible and acceptable intervention for rural breast cancer patients with insomnia and symptom clusters, warranting a randomized controlled trial to confirm efficacy. Clinicians should await stronger evidence before adopting this intervention routinely.

item.title: [6] The nucleus accumbens: an emerging modulator in anxiety disorders.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review explores the role of the nucleus accumbens (NAc) in anxiety disorders, synthesizing recent evidence on neurotransmitter systems (opioid, oxytocin, endocannabinoid), glial mechanisms, and neural circuits connecting the NAc to other brain regions. It aims to highlight the NAc as a potential therapeutic target for anxiety.
FINDINGS: The review summarizes preclinical and clinical studies suggesting that the NAc modulates anxiety through interactions with the ventral tegmental area, bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, and medial prefrontal cortex. Pharmacological agents like ketamine and non-pharmacological interventions such as exercise and deep brain stimulation are proposed as emerging treatments targeting the NAc. However, the review does not provide quantitative effect sizes, confidence intervals, or p-values.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review, this paper synthesizes diverse and emerging evidence but lacks the methodological rigor of systematic reviews or meta-analyses. The conclusions are hypothesis-generating rather than definitive, and the clinical applicability of targeting the NAc remains speculative. The review highlights promising avenues for future research but does not establish causality or clinical efficacy.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This review suggests that the NAc may be a relevant target for novel anxiety treatments, but current evidence is insufficient to guide clinical practice. Clinicians should await controlled trials before considering interventions targeting the NAc.

item.title: [32] Valerian, chamomile, and lavender for insomnia and sleep disturbance: a narrative review of mechanisms, clinical efficacy, and safety.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review synthesizes mechanistic, clinical, and safety evidence for valerian, chamomile, and lavender in adults with insomnia disorder or sleep disturbance, prioritizing randomized controlled trials, systematic reviews, and guidelines from a structured literature search.
FINDINGS: Valerian showed minimal and inconsistent effects on subjective sleep quality with no consistent impact on objective sleep latency or total sleep time; evidence quality was low. Chamomile reduced Sleep Quality scores in small, heterogeneous trials, while oral lavender oil (Silexan) appeared to improve disturbed sleep primarily by reducing anxiety in patients with anxiety disorders. Evidence varied by preparation, dose, route, and population.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is weak due to small samples, heterogeneity, and methodological limitations; no meta-analysis or formal risk-of-bias assessment was performed. Findings suggest no robust support for these botanicals as alternatives to first-line insomnia treatments. High-quality, adequately powered trials with objective outcomes and adverse-event monitoring are needed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not justify recommending valerian, chamomile, or lavender as alternatives to guideline-based insomnia treatments; clinicians should discuss use with patients, acknowledging product variability and limited efficacy data.

item.title: [25] Rethinking opioid therapy in chronic pain: Role of neurobiology.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review (2015–2025) examines the neurobiological rationale for limiting long-term opioid therapy in chronic non-cancer pain and proposes a structured, multimodal, patient-centred alternative for primary care. It synthesizes systematic reviews, RCTs, and guidelines to argue that chronic pain is primarily a CNS-mediated threat response rather than persistent nociceptive input.
FINDINGS: The review cites level I evidence that long-term opioids provide at best modest benefit for chronic pain and level I evidence of harms (tolerance, dependence, opioid-induced hyperalgesia, OUD). Level II evidence frames pain as a CNS output modulated by threat appraisal. A multimodal framework (the “5 Ps”: pain education, physical activity, psychological strategies, pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic supports) is supported by level I–II evidence for improving function.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative synthesis, this paper is not designed to yield precise effect sizes or confidence intervals. Its strength lies in integrating diverse high-quality sources to challenge opioid-first paradigms. However, narrative reviews are susceptible to selection and confirmation bias. The clinical recommendations rest on mechanistic plausibility and aggregated evidence rather than head-to-head trials of the proposed framework versus usual care. External validity hinges on primary care settings where multimodal resources are available.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: For patients with chronic pain, clinicians should prioritize non-opioid, function-focused strategies and reserve time-limited opioid trials for carefully selected cases with clear functional goals and close monitoring. Watch for escalating doses or paradoxical hyperalgesia as red flags.

item.title: [20] Psychological support for women following perinatal loss: a systematic review of clinical practice guidance.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review examined clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) to identify and appraise psychological recommendations for supporting women’s mental health after perinatal loss (pregnancy or early postnatal death). It assessed the quality of existing guidance and synthesized recommendations to highlight gaps in psychological care.
FINDINGS: Sixteen guidelines were included; ten rated “excellent,” four “good,” and two “average” in methodological quality. Recommendations covered psychological assessment, interventions, psychosocial support, service provision, and systemic factors, but consistency and specificity varied widely. Few guidelines provided clear guidance on follow-up or long-term psychological assessment.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is limited by heterogeneous and sometimes vague recommendations, with only moderate methodological quality in many guidelines. The lack of standardized, evidence-based follow-up protocols risks under-detection of mental health difficulties in grieving women. While the review identifies areas for improvement, it does not provide effect sizes or direct clinical outcomes, making it difficult to assess clinical impact.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current guidelines offer fragmented psychological support after perinatal loss. Clinicians should be aware of these gaps and consider individualized, trauma-informed follow-up, while advocating for the development of standardized, evidence-based CPGs to improve care quality.

item.title: [19] Psychiatrists' Prescribing Choice Determinants for Brexpiprazole and Other Antipsychotics in Patients With Schizophrenia: Results From a National Congress-Based Survey in Argentina.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This cross-sectional, convenience survey examined Argentine psychiatrists' self-reported antipsychotic prescribing patterns for schizophrenia, with a focus on awareness and use of brexpiprazole, clozapine, and long-acting injectable antipsychotics (LAIs). The study aimed to identify factors influencing prescribing choices in routine practice.
FINDINGS: Among 371 psychiatrists (60.1% female, mean age 38.7 years), second-generation antipsychotics (SGAs) were prescribed by 80.3% of respondents. Clozapine was used in 12.8% of patients, LAIs in 11.6%, while brexpiprazole was prescribed by only 29.1% of respondents (3.9% of total prescriptions), with limited availability, cost, and lack of experience cited as barriers. Factors most strongly associated with clozapine and LAI prescribing included higher proportions of treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TRS) patients and greater clinical exposure to schizophrenia. Key determinants for antipsychotic selection were positive symptom efficacy (90.0%), tolerability (70.0%), negative symptom efficacy (64.7%), and lower cardiometabolic risk (54.9%).
INTERPRETATION: This study provides exploratory, hypothesis-generating data on prescribing patterns in Argentina, but its cross-sectional design and reliance on self-reported data limit causal inference. The sample, drawn from a national congress, may not represent all psychiatrists, particularly those in non-academic or rural settings. The low uptake of brexpiprazole and identified barriers suggest practical constraints (e.g., cost, availability) rather than clinical preference. The findings highlight perceived challenges in schizophrenia treatment but cannot determine effectiveness or optimal prescribing strategies.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The study suggests that brexpiprazole remains underutilized in Argentina due to systemic barriers rather than clinical inefficacy. Clinicians should be aware of these constraints when considering newer SGAs. However, the lack of comparative effectiveness data means no firm treatment recommendations can be made based on this survey alone.

item.title: [18] Reducing re-hospitalization in schizophrenia: real-world comparison of first- vs. second-generation long-acting injectable antipsychotics.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study compared first-generation (FGA) versus second-generation (SGA) long-acting injectable (LAI) antipsychotics in patients with schizophrenia spectrum disorders (SSDs) to assess differences in reducing hospitalizations, relapses, and suicide attempts. This mirror-image, retrospective cohort study evaluated 133 patients over three years after switching from oral antipsychotics to LAIs.
FINDINGS: Hospital admissions decreased from 53.4% to 6.0% after LAI initiation, and the average hospitalization duration dropped from 14.26 days (±29.1) to 1.35 days (±8.09). Both FGA-LAIs and SGA-LAIs reduced hospitalizations, relapses, and suicide attempts, but no statistically significant differences were found between the two groups.
INTERPRETATION: The study demonstrates a strong association between LAI initiation and reduced hospitalizations and relapses, but the mirror-image design (pre-post comparison without a concurrent control group) limits causal inference. Residual confounding and lack of randomization weaken internal validity, and the predominantly male, middle-aged, Caucasian sample limits generalizability. The lack of difference between FGA- and SGA-LAIs suggests no clear superiority of one class over the other in this cohort.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: LAIs appear effective in reducing rehospitalizations in SSD, but the choice between FGA- and SGA-LAIs should remain individualized based on tolerability, patient preference, and clinical judgment rather than assumed superiority of one class.

item.title: [16] Psychotropic drug-induced lipid disturbances: a genome-wide association study in a Swiss psychiatric cohort.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This genome-wide association study (GWAS) in a Swiss psychiatric cohort (PsyMetab, n=829) investigated genetic variants influencing lipid changes induced by psychotropic drugs (e.g., antipsychotics, lithium, mirtazapine) over up to one year of treatment. The study aimed to identify genetic contributors to dyslipidemia in psychiatric patients, a clinically relevant issue given the metabolic side effects of these medications.
FINDINGS: Seven loci reached genome-wide significance (P < 5 × 10⁻⁸) for associations with treatment-induced lipid changes. Three variants were linked to total cholesterol changes (e.g., rs17313064 with aripiprazole/quetiapine), two to HDL-cholesterol changes (e.g., rs12097296 with lithium/mirtazapine), one to triglycerides with risperidone (rs10260518), and one to triglycerides across any drug (rs56286230). Sensitivity analyses supported the robustness of rs10933971’s effect on HDL-cholesterol across varying timeframes.
INTERPRETATION: The study’s strengths include its longitudinal design and focus on drug-specific genetic effects, but limitations include the lack of classical replication and potential confounding by heterogeneous drug exposures. The findings suggest plausible genetic targets (e.g., lipid-regulating genes) but require validation in independent cohorts. The clinical significance is unclear, as effect sizes and allele frequencies were not reported, and the study does not yet translate to actionable pharmacogenomic guidelines.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current practice remains unchanged; this is preliminary evidence for genetic predictors of psychotropic-induced dyslipidemia. Clinicians should continue monitoring metabolic parameters in patients on these drugs while awaiting further validation and clinical utility studies.

item.title: [14] Treatment response prediction in major neurocognitive disorder with depression using the scalp-to-cortex distance of TMS targets: implications for personalized dose estimation.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study asks whether scalp-to-cortex distance (SCD) of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) targets can predict antidepressant response in elderly patients with major neurocognitive disorder and depression, using data from a secondary analysis of a randomized clinical trial (RCT) with 55 participants.
FINDINGS: Responders to active 10 Hz rTMS had a greater SCD at left M1, a lower SCD_DLPFC/M1 ratio, and higher SCD-modified output difference (SCD-MOOD) than nonresponders. Logistic regression showed associations between remission and SCD of left M1 (p = 0.038) and SCD-MOOD (p = 0.042). A classification model using SCD metrics achieved 92.5% accuracy at week 3 and 86.2% at week 12. The model showed strong specificity for distinguishing active from sham stimulation.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is preliminary and based on a small secondary analysis of an RCT with no correction for multiple comparisons. The high accuracy metrics may reflect overfitting in a small sample (n=55) and require external validation. The clinical utility of SCD-based prediction remains uncertain until replicated in larger, adequately powered studies with longer follow-up and blinding integrity checks.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings do not justify changing routine practice. SCD metrics may one day guide personalized TMS dosing, but further validation is needed before considering adoption in clinical settings.

item.title: [12] Microdosing Approach for Switching From Methadone to Buprenorphine in Opioid Disorder: A French Case Series.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examined whether a 14-day microdosing protocol can facilitate switching from methadone to buprenorphine in patients with opioid use disorder in routine French outpatient settings, addressing the challenge of withdrawal during conventional induction. This case series reports on 10 patients treated at two specialist addiction centers in Lyon, France.
FINDINGS: Of 10 patients (8 men, 2 women), 6 (60%) successfully completed the transition using the microdosing protocol, including five outpatients. Withdrawal symptoms were absent or mild in successful transfers. Two patients discontinued due to withdrawal symptoms, and two were lost to follow-up. No severe adverse events were reported.
